title: The Inquisition
hookLine: converts are watched and tried; some keep Judaism in secret

cards: Friday evening in a Spanish city. A family that has been Christian on paper for years sits down to dinner. Before sunset the mother changed the tablecloth and put on clean linen.

Somewhere out of sight, perhaps inside a jar, perhaps in a cellar, a small lamp is burning. Nobody says why. Across the street, a neighbor notices the clean linen and the smokeless chimney on Saturday.
That neighbor may soon be asked to tell what they saw.

teach.b: Back to Spain, and the riots. In those riots and the years after, Jews converted to Christianity, some under threat of death, some under pressure, some by their own choice.
In Spanish they were called conversos, converts, or New Christians. Some became devoted Catholics. Some kept parts of Jewish life in secret.
Others lived somewhere in between. Hebrew sources call those forced into baptism anusim, the ones who were compelled. Suspicion fell on conversos as a group.
The Spanish Inquisition was a tribunal set up under the Spanish crown, with the pope's approval, to root out heresy among the baptized.
Its authority was over Christians, so in its early years its chief target was the converso, the Christian suspected of still being a Jew.

teach.h: LISTS OF SIGNS TO WATCH FOR.
teach.b: It published lists of signs to watch for: candles on Friday night, clean clothes for the Sabbath, refusing pork, fasting on the Day of Atonement, washing a body for burial in the Jewish way.
Neighbors and servants were invited to come forward. Trials followed, with property seized, families shamed, and some of the accused burned.
Sincere Christians were caught up too, because a family's past was enough to make it suspect. So what was hidden faith?
Sometimes a few customs kept without words: a grandmother lighting a candle out of sight, a prayer whispered in a mixture of languages.
Tradition says some families kept such customs for generations, long after anyone remembered the reason.
This week followed Jews out of England, through the plague years, into Poland and its little towns, through Yiddish and Glückel's pages.
It ends here, with faith kept behind a closed door.

how: Jewish communities remember the anusim, the forced converts, in study and storytelling, and some descendants of conversos today are exploring and reclaiming their Jewish roots.

games.q: you are a converso. it's Friday evening, and the Inquisition has published a list of signs to watch for. what does a family keeping hidden faith do?
o: light candles openly in the window.
keep a small lamp out of sight, perhaps in a jar or a cellar.
games.why: some kept customs quietly, out of sight, and tradition says some families kept them for generations.

practice: Think of the people, in every age and every tradition, who have had to keep what they believed out of sight: someone keeping a fast at a work lunch without a word, a person reading scripture on a phone under a desk.
Just keep them company for a moment, and if you pray, remember them in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Converso. A Jew who became a Christian in Spain or Portugal, by force, pressure or choice, and who could be watched, accused and tried for keeping Jewish ways. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: anusim, the ones who were compelled, forced converts.

carryVoice: Your line: hidden faith. Some customs outlived the memory of why they were kept. See you tomorrow.
